#9 [paper] Neural Conditional Gaussian Model: Efficient Data Assimilation with Sequential Uncertainty Quantification for Nonlinear Dynamics
Authors: Chuan-Qi Chen, Nan Chen
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/8e67a1a0cfbd444d5ad1c36af1dd8747f61f9917
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Conventional nonlinear filtering for data assimilation in partially observed nonlinear systems is computationally expensive and often requires an explicit dynamical model.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), which maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space with a conditional Gaussian structure for closed-form updates, using a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections to map latent posterior…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems.
Abstract:
Data assimilation (DA) in partially observed nonlinear systems requires repeated estimation of both hidden states and their uncertainty. Conventional nonlinear filtering can be computationally expensive and often relies on an explicit dynamical model. In this paper, we develop the Neural Conditional Gaussian Model (Neural CGM), a data-driven dynamical model that maps unobserved physical states into a learned latent space, where the dynamics of the latent states follow a conditional Gaussian structure. This structure allows closed-form DA updates in the latent space, while nonlinear encoder-decoder mappings retain the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamics in physical space. A key feature of Neural CGM is its treatment of uncertainty in DA. The latent posterior mean and covariance are mapped to the physical variables through a Gaussian decoder that combines local moment propagation with learned nonlinear corrections. The resulting physical-space posterior statistics depend on the sequentially updated latent distribution rather than on a separate post-processing estimate. The same statistics enter a Gaussian negative log-likelihood during training, so both the posterior mean and uncertainty affect the learned model. Because Neural CGM learns the dynamical model itself, it can also be used for state forecasting and simulation without explicit knowledge of the governing equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark nonlinear dynamical systems show accurate state estimation and forecasting while substantially reducing online assimilation cost relative to conventional nonlinear DA methods. Neural CGM is therefore suited to repeated state estimation, uncertainty quantification, and prediction from partial observations.

Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

#15 [paper] Local adaptation expands genetic variation in the thermal performance of a coastal fish: Implications for ocean warming.
Authors: Lundquist, Alexis J, Cole, Thea R, Johnson, Darren W
Venue: Ecology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43034912/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): To determine how local adaptation to climate conditions maintains or expands genetic variation in thermal performance traits within a metapopulation, and to assess the implications for responses to ocean warming.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Experimental breeding design using gametes from three coastal fish populations (California Grunion) separated by ~150 km. Offspring were reared in a common laboratory environment across a gradient of temperatures. Genetic variation and heritability for growth and mortality rates were quantified usi…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Three local populations of the California Grunion (a coastal fish) along a north-south cline, reared in a common laboratory environment.
Abstract:
Species' responses to climate change can include a component of contemporary evolution, and such responses can be important in offsetting the detrimental effects of warming. However, the capacity of populations to evolve will depend on the level of genetic variation underlying traits affected by climate change. It is not always clear how such variation is maintained, but one plausible mechanism involves adaptation of subpopulations to local climate conditions. In this study, we experimentally tested whether populations of a coastal fish, the California Grunion, exhibited inherited differences in thermal reaction norms (measured as the family-average values of growth and mortality across a range of temperatures). We also quantified the degree to which differentiation among locations increased the amount of genetic variation underlying thermal reaction norms within the population at large. We collected gametes from three local populations that were separated by an average of 150 km and located along a north-south cline. Eggs from each population were fertilized in a breeding experiment that allowed us to quantify genetic variation and heritability. Larvae from all three populations were reared in a common laboratory environment and across temperatures reflecting their natural range. Patterns of growth exhibited inherited differences in that offspring from higher latitude populations grew faster on average when reared in identical conditions. Offspring from different source populations varied significantly in how sensitive their mortality rates were to temperature, and offspring from parents in the lowest latitude population had lower mortality rates at high temperatures. When growth and mortality rates were combined to express biomass, we saw evidence of both counter gradient variation (greater production from high-latitude populations) and local adaptation in thermal specialization (peak production occurred at higher temperatures for the lowest latitude population). Genetic variation among locations increased the total amount of genetic variation within the broader metapopulation. Even when considering only three subpopulations, broad-sense heritability values were increased for both growth and mortality rate by factors of 1.07 and 1.1, respectively. Our results emphasize that metapopulation-level processes can play important roles in both the promotion of genetic variation and the response to selection generated by climate change.

results.content:
#13 [paper] VMCF: VMamba–CNN Fusion Network for Sea Surface Temperature Prediction
Authors: Hao Zhan, Xiaoyan Li, Pengfei Lin, Xueming Zhu, Jiuke Wang, Jane You
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213846
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Accurate short-term sea surface temperature (SST) forecasting, specifically addressing the limitations of CNN-based methods in capturing global spatiotemporal dependencies and the high computational costs of Transformer-based approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): VMCF (VMamba–CNN Fusion Network), a dual-branch architecture that combines CNNs for local feature extraction with VMamba for efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation, strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): OISST dataset.
Abstract:
Sea surface temperature (SST) exerts a critical influence on diverse physical and biological processes within the marine environment. Nevertheless, accurate short-term SST forecasting still remains challenging. Current deep learning (DL) models have two key limitations: first, the convolutional neural network (CNN)-based methods fail to capture global spatiotemporal dependencies; second, Transformer-based approaches suffer from relatively high computational costs. To address these issues, this study introduces a VMamba–CNN fusion network (VMCF), a dual-branch architecture designed to effectively characterize the multiscale temporal and spatial variability of SST. The VMCF combines the powerful local feature extraction capability of CNNs with the efficient linear-computability global spatiotemporal representation of VMamba, further strengthened via channel-wise feature fusion. Extensive experiments on the OISST dataset demonstrate significant performance improvements across all evaluation metrics, clearly validating the superiority of VMCF in SST forecasting. Specifically, it achieves root-mean-square error (RMSE) values ranging from 0.17 °C to 0.51 °C across 1–10-day lead times, outperforming five state-of-the-art DL models.

results.content:
#12 [paper] Evaluation of direct assimilation of brightness temperature to update Arctic sea-ice model fields
Authors: Marina Durán Moro, Thomas Lavergne, Laurent Bertino, Cyril Palerme, Yue Ying, Jiping Xie, Atle Macdonald Sørensen
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-6669
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Traditional assimilation of sea-ice concentration (SIC) derived from brightness temperature (Tb) observations violates Gaussian assumptions, introduces inconsistencies in the marginal ice zone, and loses sea-ice age information.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Direct assimilation of Level-1 Tb observations using an Ensemble Kalman Filter and a radiative transfer model (RTM) with four emissivity parameterizations: fixed, Atlas-based climatology, Distance Along the Line (DAL), and a machine learning approach.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Arctic coupled ocean-sea-ice numerical model during a winter season using AMSR2 satellite mission data.
Abstract:
Abstract. Traditionally, sea-ice concentration (SIC) derived from satellite brightness temperature (Tb) observations is assimilated in operational ocean prediction systems. However, SIC is a bounded variable, which violates the Gaussian assumptions commonly used in data assimilation. Moreover, different algorithms for retrieval of sea-ice variables often introduce inconsistencies, particularly in the marginal ice zone (MIZ). Also, the valuable sea-ice age information inherent in Tb measurements is lost in the SIC product. In this study, we investigate the direct assimilation of Level-1 Tb observations from the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer (AMSR2) satellite mission into an Arctic coupled ocean-sea-ice numerical model during a winter season. Since Tb is not a model variable, a radiative transfer model (RTM) is implemented, incorporating four parameterizations for the effective emissivity over sea-ice areas. These include a fixed parameterization with constant values across the region, an Atlas-based climatology parameterization, a new method based on a Distance Along the Line (DAL) computation, and a machine learning approach. We evaluate each parameterization by comparing the RTM-simulated Tbs to the AMSR2 Tbs. The DAL-based parametrization yields the best results, with mean absolute differences less than 4 K. Then, the assimilation is performed through a series of standalone analyses using the Ensemble Kalman Filter to update the sea-ice forecast fields by running five different experiments, one assimilating a high-resolution SIC product (SIRANO), and the others assimilating AMSR2 Tbs using the four different RTM parameterizations. When the resulting analyses are compared to SIRANO SIC, the DAL experiment shows the lowest differences. This is corroborated by the comparison to another SIC product (Bremen ARTIST Sea Ice). In the MIZ, the Tb-assimilation experiments demonstrate a 2–9 % reduction in the mean absolute difference compared to the AMSR2 SIC observations (SIRANO and Bremen) relative to the SIC-assimilation experiment. These findings are encouraging and highlight the potential of assimilating Level-1 Tb observations to improve sea-ice analyses and forecasts.

final_text:
#1 fits the Marine heatwave early warning (#3) project better — but neither is a strong fit, and I'd want to be clear about that.

**What fits**

- **#1** is about strengthening the global ocean observing system: deploying observation equipment, running observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), and network optimization, with a focus on EOVs and data delivery. That is adjacent to the project's core — ML-corrected ensembles and a dashboard built on ocean observations — and it is the only one of the two that touches observation/data infrastructure at all.
- **#2** is about the Antarctic and Southern Ocean: near/mid/long-term projections, sea ice, ice shelves, bottom water formation, and polar ecosystem vulnerability. The project is a 2–6 week marine heatwave forecast for the regional coast. The setting is a different region entirely, and the timescales (decadal to millennial) are far from the project's subseasonal horizon.

**What does not**

- Neither call is a forecasting call. #1 is about observing infrastructure and governance, not about predicting marine heatwaves; #2 is about polar climate projections, not regional coastal forecasting.
- #1's scope is global/beyond-national-jurisdiction and biodiversity-oriented; the project is a regional, fisheries-facing forecasting product. #2's scope is polar and multidisciplinary, with no coastal-forecasting angle.
- #1's deadline is 2027-02-16 (about two and a half months out), which is tight for a project that is 60% done with a dashboard still in testing. #2's deadline is 2027-09-23, but the fit is worse.

**What I could not check**

- Eligibility for either call (institution type, career stage, consortium requirements) — I have no eligibility details for either.
- Whether the project's members (Mara, Tomás, Sun-hee) have the expertise either call needs — I have not looked at their profiles.

**Bottom line:** #1 is the better of the two, mainly because it is the only one that touches ocean observation and data infrastructure, which is the project's foundation. But it is a weak fit — it is a global observing-system call, not a marine heatwave forecasting call. #2 is a poor fit on region and timescale. If the real question is whether either is worth pursuing, the honest answer is that neither is a natural home for this project; #1 is the less-bad option, and the tight deadline makes it harder to act on.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

final_text:
#14 matters most for Plastic pathways (#1).

It is the only item in the slate that is about the project's core problem: a tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter, built for OceanParcels 3.1.4 and applied to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea (Sehan Lim, Sunwook Hong, Zenodo, 2026). The project's focus is tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches, and its current status is that the beaching model is being checked against last summer's beach surveys — #14 is essentially the same kind of tool, with the same beaching question, so it is the most directly relevant paper in the feed. It also ships the code, scripts and aggregated results, so it is usable, not just readable.

The closest second is #11, satellite observations of river plumes and wind response (Sentinel-2/Sentinel-3, Iceland), which speaks to the river-mouth/satellite-detection side of the project. The rest of the slate — #5, #6, #7, #8, #9, #10, #12, #13 — is about diatoms, thermal stress, data assimilation, SST reanalysis and chlorophyll estimation, which is adjacent to the lab's interests but not to this project's debris-tracking problem.

One caveat: the slate ranks #14 tenth of ten, so the ranking itself does not put it first. But on fit to the project's stated focus and current work, it is the one I'd read first.

Authors: Michael Whitney, Luke C. Glass
Venue: Mendeley Data

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Determining the distribution of the Skjálfandafljót and Jökulsá á Fjöllum river plumes and characterizing their response to various wind directions and low-wind conditions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Sentinel-2 True Color and Sentinel-3 Total Suspended Matter (TSM) satellite imagery.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Skjálfandi and Öxarfjörður bays on Iceland’s Arctic Ocean coast.
Abstract:
This dataset contains the supporting data for figures in “Satellite Observations of River Plumes and Wind Response in Neighboring Bays on Iceland’s Northeast Coast,” a manuscript for Regional Studies in Marine Science by Michael M. Whitney and Luke C. Glass (affiliated with the University of Connecticut). This study analyzes the Skjálfandafljót river plume in Skjálfandi and the Jökulsá á Fjöllum plume in Öxarfjörður, on Iceland’s Arctic Ocean coast. These freshwaters influence ecosystems that support cetaceans, ecotourism, and fisheries. Study objectives are 1) determining plume distributions with True Color and Total Suspended Matter (TSM) satellite imagery, 2) describing low-wind plume characteristics, and 3) characterizing response to a variety of wind directions. The approach is applicable to river plumes around the world and findings can help inform new studies, monitoring, and marine protection efforts. The dataset includes MATLAB data files that contain all the output data presented in the corresponding figures within the manuscript. Details about variables and units are described within the figure captions and manuscript text. Zipped files of the Sentinel-2 True Color and Sentinel-3 TSM satellite images (downloaded from the online Copernicus Browser and analyzed) also are included. The manuscript contains complete descriptions of methods, analysis, and interpretation. final_text:
I have both calls and the project. Here's the comparison.

**#1 — Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
- Setting: global ocean observing frameworks — IOC-GOOS, areas beyond national jurisdiction, Copernicus Marine Service.
- Aims: strengthen/expand observing networks, deploy equipment, OSEs/OSSEs, network optimization, technology roadmaps.
- Fit with #3 (Marine heatwave early warning): the project is a 2–6 week ML-corrected ensemble forecast for the regional coast, delivered to fisheries managers via a public dashboard. #1 is about *observing infrastructure and data delivery*, not forecasting — but it is the same family of work (ocean data, services, delivery to users). The project's dashboard and hindcast work could plausibly contribute to observing-system/data-delivery outcomes, though the call's focus is on equipment, networks and governance, not subseasonal forecasting.

**#2 — Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
- Setting: Antarctic continental shelves and bottom-water formation regions; near/mid/long-term projections, sea ice, ESMs, biodiversity monitoring.
- Fit with #3: essentially none. The project is a regional coastal marine-heatwave forecast; #2 is about polar projections and cryosphere/ocean interactions. Different region, different timescales, different methods.

**Which fits better: #1.** It is the closer of the two, but it is still a stretch — the call is about strengthening the observing system, not about subseasonal forecasting or fisheries-facing dashboards. #2 is a poor fit on region and scope.

**Strongest reason:** #1's setting (ocean observing, data delivery, Copernicus-type services) is the same domain as #3's dashboard and data-assimilation work; #2's Antarctic/Southern Ocean focus has no overlap with a regional coastal heatwave forecast.

**Biggest doubt:** #1's expected outcomes center on observing-system strengthening and governance, not on forecast products — the project's ML-corrected ensemble and public dashboard are not what the call asks for, so a fit would need to be argued, not assumed.

**What I could not check:** eligibility rules (career stage, institution type, citizenship) for either call — not visible in what I read. Also the project's confirmed state is "never confirmed by its members" (#3), so its milestones are not formally locked.

One more note: #1's deadline (2027-02-16) is about two and a half months away, which is tight for a project whose dashboard is still in testing with two fisheries offices.

# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,

3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.

I read both calls and the project. Here's the comparison.

**Project #3 (Marine heatwave early warning):** a 2–6 week forecast of marine heatwaves for the regional coast, from an ML-corrected ensemble, delivered to fisheries managers through a public dashboard. Hindcasts for 2015–2024 beat persistence at four weeks; dashboard in testing with two fisheries offices. Research areas: marine heatwave prediction, ocean data assimilation, ocean data dashboards.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16):** aims to strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system — deployment of observation equipment, observing system experiments, network optimisation, Copernicus/GOOS governance, with attention to biodiversity and under-observed regions. It is about the observing infrastructure and data backbone, not about forecasting or regional applications.

**#2 — Unlocking a safe operating space for Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23):** resolves uncertainties and projections for the Antarctic/Southern Ocean — ocean–atmosphere–ice interactions, ESMs, monitoring indicators, ecosystem vulnerability. The setting is polar, not the regional coast.

**Which fits better: #1, but only loosely.** The project's core is ocean data assimilation and observing-system-adjacent work, and #1 is squarely about ocean observing capacity, data delivery and services — the same family of problems. #2 is a polar-region call; its setting (Antarctic shelves, bottom water formation, Southern Ocean) is a different region and a different problem (climate projections and ecosystem vulnerability), so it fits the project much less well.

**What does not fit in either:** neither call is about marine heatwave prediction or subseasonal forecasting for a regional coast, and neither is about fisheries-manager dashboards. #1 is about strengthening the observing system itself, not applying it to forecasts; #2 is about polar climate projections. Neither is a natural home for this project as it stands.

**Deadlines:** #1 closes 2027-02-16 (about two and a half months out), #2 closes 2027-09-23.

**What I could not check:** eligibility rules (career stage, institution type, citizenship) for either call — the corpus text does not state them, so I have not guessed. Also, the project's confirmed state is never confirmed by its members, so I am comparing against the focus statement and progress as recorded, not a signed-off plan.

One plain sentence on the strongest reason: #1 is the closer fit because it is about ocean observing capacity and data delivery, which is the same family of work as the project's data-assimilation and dashboard goals. One on the biggest doubt: neither call is actually about marine heatwave forecasting, so fitting either would mean re-scoping the project toward observing-system or polar-climate work, which is a real change.

I have both calls and the project. Here is the comparison.

**#1 — Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16)**
- Aims: strengthen and operationalise the global ocean observing system (GOOS), deployment of observation equipment, OSEs/OSSEs, network optimisation, Copernicus services, areas beyond national jurisdiction.
- Overlap with #3: ocean observations and data delivery are adjacent to what the project does — an ML-corrected ensemble for 2–6 week marine heatwave forecasts delivered to fisheries managers. But the call is about global observing infrastructure and governance, not regional forecasting or early warning. The project's method (subseasonal ML-corrected ensembles, dashboards) is not what this call funds.

**#2 — Antarctica and the Southern Ocean (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23)**
- Aims: projections of the Antarctic/Southern Ocean region, sea ice, bottom water formation, ESMs, decadal-to-millennial timescales, polar ecosystems.
- Overlap with #3: essentially none. Different region (polar vs. regional coast), different timescales (decadal+ vs. 2–6 weeks), different purpose (climate projections vs. early warning).

**Which fits better: #1, but only weakly.** It is the closer of the two because it is about ocean observation and data systems rather than a specific polar region, but it is still a stretch — the project is a regional forecasting and dashboard effort, not a global observing-system build. #2 is a poor fit on region, timescale and purpose.

One more thing worth flagging: #1's deadline is 2027-02-16, about three weeks away, and it is a €50M global-infrastructure call — the project's scope (a regional ML forecasting pipeline) is far from what it funds. I could not check eligibility (institution type, consortium requirements) from what I read, so I would not treat either as a realistic application without verifying the call's eligibility rules.

If you want, I can check the project's feed (#3) to see whether either of these is already in its slate, or look at what the lab's feed holds for marine heatwave/subseasonal forecasting instead.

**#1 — Global Ocean Observing System (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16).** Its aims — strengthening and operationalising ocean observing networks, deploying observation equipment, running observing system experiments, and improving data delivery for services like Copernicus — sit close to what #3 does: it turns ocean observations into forecasts (ML-corrected ensembles, hindcasts beating persistence at four weeks) and delivers them to managers via a dashboard. results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- scientists, public authorities and businesses benefit from strengthened and resilient global ocean observing capacities, coordinated under the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission’s Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS),[1] through the deployment of ocean observation equipment, in particular for the provision of critical observations for marine biodiversity and ecosystem knowledge;

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Scope:

The EU has committed to global leadership in climate action, biodiversity protection and ocean governance, notably through the EU Ocean Pact, the EU Ocean Observation Initiative “OceanEye”, the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the EU Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters, the EU Climate Law, and international commitments such as the Global Biodiversity Framework and Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ). Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

Sustained and resilient ocean observation is crucial for marine biodiversity conservation and restoration under a changing climate, meaning that maintaining an optimised global ocean observing system is very important to achieve biodiversity goals.

Evolving geopolitical dynamics and reduced engagement by key international partners pose significant risks to the continuity, openness and resilience of global ocean observing systems, in particular in areas beyond national jurisdictions, highlighting the need for reinforced European action to safeguard scientific sovereignty and long-term, reliable observations and predictions. final_text:
I have both grants and the project. Here's the comparison.

**#1 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System** (€50M, deadline 2027-02-16, still open) fits the Marine heatwave early warning project (#3) better.

**Why #1 fits:**
- The project (#3) is a 2–6-week marine heatwave forecast for the regional coast, built on an ML-corrected ensemble, delivered to fisheries managers through a public dashboard. Its research areas are marine heatwave prediction, ocean data assimilation, and ocean data dashboards.
- #1 is about strengthening the global ocean observing system — deployment of observation equipment, observing system experiments (OSEs/OSSEs), network optimization, and data delivery — with a focus on the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission's GOOS and Copernicus Marine Service (#1). That is the same world as the project's data-assimilation and dashboard work: better, resilient observations feeding forecasts and services.
- It is also ranked higher in the project's own slate (#1 is #2 in the slate, #2 is #4).

**Why #2 does not fit as well:**
- #2 (€5–11M, deadline 2027-09-23, still open) is about the Antarctic and Southern Ocean — near/mid/long-term projections (∼2030, 2050–2060, after ∼2060), sea ice, ice shelves, bottom water formation, and cryosphere dynamics (#2). The project is a regional-coast, 2–6-week subseasonal forecast. The timescales and regions barely overlap.

**Strongest reason:** #1 is about the observing and data-delivery infrastructure that a forecasting project like #3 depends on; #2 is about long-term polar projections.

**Biggest doubt:** #1 is a €50M global-scale call about strengthening GOOS and biodiversity/ecosystem observations — it is not a forecasting call, and the project's specific ML-corrected-ensemble, fisheries-dashboard work is not what it funds. So "fits better" is relative, not a strong fit.

**What I could not check:** eligibility rules (career stage, institution type, citizenship) for either call — the corpus item does not state them, so I won't guess. Also, the project's confirmed state is "never confirmed by its members" (#3), so I am comparing against the focus statement and progress note, not a locked-in plan.

One more note: #1's deadline (2027-02-16) is much sooner than #2's (2027-09-23), so if the lab wants to move, #1 is the tighter window.

I have enough to answer. Here's the honest picture.

**Best fit: #6 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation** (€50,000,000, deadline 2027-02-16, still open). It is the only open grant in #1's slate that touches the project's core — ocean observing, data assimilation and resilience — and it is the one the nightly ranking points at the lab's people. The project's problem (a 2–6 week marine heatwave forecast from an ML-corrected ensemble, delivered to fisheries managers) is not literally what #6 funds, though: #6 is about strengthening and operationalising the global observing system (deployment of observation equipment, OSEs/OSSEs, network optimisation), not about forecasting or dashboards. So the fit is real but partial — the project's dashboard and fisheries-delivery side has no home in any of the ten slate grants.

The other nine do not fit: #5 is instrumentation development, #7 is carbon sources/sinks, #8 is Antarctic/Southern Ocean, #9 is biodiversity data integration, #10 is marine geology, #11 is blue forest ecosystems, #12/#13 are wave/tidal energy, #14 is hypersonic modeling. None of them is about marine heatwave prediction, subseasonal forecasting or ocean data dashboards.

**Who should lead:** #2 Mara Ellison (you) — you declared ocean data assimilation, which is the one slot #6 asks for that you cover, and you're the PI. #17 Priya Raman covers the same slot via satellite ocean remote sensing. #3 Tomás Ferreira-Lind and #4 Sun-hee Park are the closest profile matches in the ranking (65% and 63%) but neither covers a named slot for #6 — Tomás's declared interests are circulation/turbulence and physics-informed ML, Sun-hee's are ocean data tools. I'd suggest you lead with Priya as the co-lead on the observing/remote-sensing side, with Tomás and Sun-hee contributing the forecasting and dashboard work.

**Outside the lab:** I can't name anyone. Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, and the who-should-apply skill only allows outside-the-lab suggestions when that search is on and people have consented. I also have no co-authorship path from you to anyone outside the lab (I checked #3 and found none). What you can do in the app: turn on collaborator search and check consent, or ask the lab's members to suggest partners.

**Gaps worth flagging:** #1's concepts include "works on fisheries" and "sea surface temperature" — neither is declared by any member, so the fisheries-delivery side of the project is uncovered. And #6's slots for OSEs/OSSEs, network optimisation and areas beyond national jurisdiction are uncovered by anyone in the lab.

One doubt to be plain about: #6 is a €50M, multi-year, global-observing-system call, not a grant for a regional heatwave forecasting project. If the goal is funding the project itself, none of the ten slate grants is a clean fit — #6 is the closest, not a match.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

- Better understanding of oceanic carbon dioxide (CO2) sources and sinks, their drivers and dynamics under different climate scenarios, including their responses to human interventions;

- Better understanding of land ecosystem CO2 sources and sinks, their drivers (both natural and anthropogenic) and their evolution under future climate and land-based mitigation scenarios;

- Progress on reconciling estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions and removals from land originating from the climate science and national emissions reporting communities;

- More consistent representation and quantification of lateral transfers of carbon.

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Proposals are expected to address only one of the three areas identified below - which should be clearly indicated, while ensuring coordination and cooperation across projects to address consistency in key factors, such as data, scenarios and models used or the representation of lateral transport of carbon (e.g., through river transport or harvest). Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice, specialised analytical expertise and data. This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the Carbon Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. To this end, proposals should foresee sufficient means for effective coordination (i.e. cluster meetings, joint data management, potential joint actions).

International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

Area A: Oceanic CO2 sources and sinks

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. #13 [grant] Self-Sustaining Wave Energy Capture for Persistent Autonomous Ocean-Going Systems
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13132
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles require a reliable, self-sustaining power source for recharging when operating far from human contact, specifically a wave energy capture device (WECD) that is portable, deployable in various depths, and stealthy.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Open water environments ranging from depths of 100 meters to full ocean depth, with sea states ranging from calm to Sea State 8.
Abstract:
Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water.

The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD’s design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.

Ocean weather conditions can be challenging. The WECD should function reliably at Sea State 6 or less (very rough seas, with wave heights of 4 to 6 meters), and it should be able to survive conditions up to Sea State 8 (very high seas, with wave heights of 9 to 14 meters).

ONR assumes the WECD will be tethered to some device at or near the surface of the water. That tethered system may be an autonomous vehicle in loiter mode, and since loitering involves continuous vehicle movement, the WECD should operate reliably while in motion, and its design should leverage such motion to increase energy capture.

The WECD should produce a minimum of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per day, but more is highly desirable. ONR believes 100+ kWh per day is achievable. Even in calm seas, the ideal WECD should produce sufficient electricity to charge a 2-kWh battery in 6 hours or less. Vehicle movement may be considered when ensuring this minimum level of power generation.

The desired WECD may be needed in areas where human assembly is impractical. Thus, the deliverables must include a prototype device capable of deploying the assembled WECD from the deck of a medium or large autonomous surface vessel. Like the WECD itself, the deployment device (DD) should function reliably in challenging weather conditions: Sea State 4 or less (moderate seas with wave heights of 1.25 to 2.5 meters).

Once deployed, very little of the WECD itself should be visible at the surface of the water. The WECD should minimize any increase in the visibility of the vehicle it is tethered to. This includes surface and airborne observation, both optically and by radar. Acoustic noise generated by the WECD should either be minimized or disguised to seem environmental or biological.

Cost for the WECD and associated DD should be minimized. ONR expects that under certain environmental conditions or mission requirements, WECDs may not be recoverable. At full-rate production, the ideal price will allow for multiple units per million dollars.

Under normal operating conditions, including Sea States of 6 or less, the expected operational duration of the deployed WECD should be at least one month, with three months or more expected if Sea State 4 or less is maintained.

#14 [grant] Modeling UV/VIS/near-IR Observables of Dim Hypersonic Configurations
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13091
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current physical modeling tools, specifically the JANNAF EPSS suite, lack the chemical and physical mechanisms necessary to simultaneously predict at-source UV, VIS, and near-IR radiative emissions for dim hypersonic threats.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Enhancing the JANNAF suite infrastructure by adding thermal protection system response characterization, material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models, and molecular band models for UV, VIS, and near-IR radiative emission, integrated with Navier-Stokes CFD…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Hypersonic configurations (boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions at high Mach numbers across continuum and rarefied altitudes.
Abstract:
To address dim hypersonic threats in missile defense scenarios, the government desires to enhance current physical modeling tools with the ability to simultaneously predict at-source observable properties in the ultraviolet (UV), visible (VIS), and near-infrared (near-IR) spectral regimes that are founded and built upon Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) techniques and which accounts for, but is not limited to, vehicle surface heating and ablation, Arrhenius and collisional chemically reacting flows, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects, boost and divert jet exhaust interactions with the hypersonic body flowfield, and electro-optical radiative transfer physics-based models. The modeling suite provided by the Joint Army-Navy-NASA Air Force (JANNAF) Exhaust Plume and Signatures Subcommittee (EPSS) [1-4] computes RF and certain IR observables. It is founded on CFD and DSMC flowfield codes, hardbody heating models, and radiative transfer / radar propagation techniques. However, the suite does not model all the underlying chemical and physical mechanisms needed to account for radiative emissions in the identified parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Phenomenologies that must be enhanced within or added to the suite include, but are not limited to: characterization of thermal protection system response, development of material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models that consistently apply across the continuum and rarefied regimes, and generation of molecular band models for UV, Visible, and near-IR radiative emission. The developed models should be compatible with the JANNAF suite infrastructure. And the resulting assemblage should be able to model realistic hypersonic configurations (such as boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions lasting tens of minutes with high Mach within the atmosphere over a wide range of continuum and rarefied altitudes. The resulting capability is expected to facilitate the acquisition and tracking of dim hypersonic threats in modeling and simulation venues, such as MDA’s existing agency framework, and operational scenarios.

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

Scope:

Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

- Better understanding of oceanic carbon dioxide (CO2) sources and sinks, their drivers and dynamics under different climate scenarios, including their responses to human interventions;

- Better understanding of land ecosystem CO2 sources and sinks, their drivers (both natural and anthropogenic) and their evolution under future climate and land-based mitigation scenarios;

- Progress on reconciling estimates of anthropogenic CO2 emissions and removals from land originating from the climate science and national emissions reporting communities;

- More consistent representation and quantification of lateral transfers of carbon.

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

Proposals are expected to address only one of the three areas identified below - which should be clearly indicated, while ensuring coordination and cooperation across projects to address consistency in key factors, such as data, scenarios and models used or the representation of lateral transport of carbon (e.g., through river transport or harvest). Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice, specialised analytical expertise and data. This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the Carbon Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects that will be selected under ESA’s FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. To this end, proposals should foresee sufficient means for effective coordination (i.e. cluster meetings, joint data management, potential joint actions).

International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

Area A: Oceanic CO2 sources and sinks

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. Projects are expected to improve the understanding and quantification of the various mechanisms involved, with a focus on the behaviour of the ocean sink under past (including palaeo records), present and future conditions and various climate change and emission scenarios. Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

Amount: €1,000,000–€8,925,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-MISS-2027-03-OCEAN-05

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration, and management of blue forest ecosystems (marine and coastal vegetated habitats) within European sea basins to meet EU climate, biodiversity, and restoration goals.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Innovative multidisciplinary projects integrating active and passive restoration, conservation efforts (e.g., managing Marine Protected Areas), innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., nature credits), multi-sensor research and monitoring, and community engagement, tailored to specific sea basins.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European sea basins, specifically one of four 'lighthouse' areas: Atlantic and Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic and North Sea, or Danube River basin (including Black Sea), involving EU Member States and Associated Countries.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Increased area and improved condition of marine and coastal vegetated habitats within EU waters through effective on-site conservation, restoration and management of activities to help deliver on the objectives of the Nature Restoration Regulation;

- Maintained and enhanced capacity of blue carbon ecosystems to naturally store carbon, supporting EU climate mitigation goals;

- Enhanced capacity of marine vegetated habitats/blue carbon ecosystems to support biodiversity and fisheries;

- Established novel financing and incentive mechanisms that support conservation, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems projects;

- Raised public awareness and improved community participation in blue forest ecosystems protection, restoration and management activities, ensuring long-term involvement.

Scope:

This topic seeks innovative multidisciplinary projects that will advance large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems, focusing on the assessment of ecological interactions, restoration of degraded ecosystems, conservation, and sustainable management within European sea basins. Projects are required to develop collaborations with EU Member States and Associated Countries national and regional agencies and authorities and policy makers and engage with local communities, researchers and NGOs. #14 [grant] Self-Sustaining Wave Energy Capture for Persistent Autonomous Ocean-Going Systems
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13132
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles require a reliable, self-sustaining power source for recharging when operating far from human contact, specifically a wave energy capture device (WECD) that is portable, deployable in various depths, and stealthy.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Open water environments ranging from depths of 100 meters to full ocean depth, with sea states ranging from calm to Sea State 8.
Abstract:
Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water.

The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD’s design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.

Ocean weather conditions can be challenging. The WECD should function reliably at Sea State 6 or less (very rough seas, with wave heights of 4 to 6 meters), and it should be able to survive conditions up to Sea State 8 (very high seas, with wave heights of 9 to 14 meters).

ONR assumes the WECD will be tethered to some device at or near the surface of the water. That tethered system may be an autonomous vehicle in loiter mode, and since loitering involves continuous vehicle movement, the WECD should operate reliably while in motion, and its design should leverage such motion to increase energy capture.

The WECD should produce a minimum of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per day, but more is highly desirable. ONR believes 100+ kWh per day is achievable. Even in calm seas, the ideal WECD should produce sufficient electricity to charge a 2-kWh battery in 6 hours or less. Vehicle movement may be considered when ensuring this minimum level of power generation.

The desired WECD may be needed in areas where human assembly is impractical. Thus, the deliverables must include a prototype device capable of deploying the assembled WECD from the deck of a medium or large autonomous surface vessel. Like the WECD itself, the deployment device (DD) should function reliably in challenging weather conditions: Sea State 4 or less (moderate seas with wave heights of 1.25 to 2.5 meters).

Once deployed, very little of the WECD itself should be visible at the surface of the water. The WECD should minimize any increase in the visibility of the vehicle it is tethered to. This includes surface and airborne observation, both optically and by radar. Acoustic noise generated by the WECD should either be minimized or disguised to seem environmental or biological.

Cost for the WECD and associated DD should be minimized. ONR expects that under certain environmental conditions or mission requirements, WECDs may not be recoverable. At full-rate production, the ideal price will allow for multiple units per million dollars.

Under normal operating conditions, including Sea States of 6 or less, the expected operational duration of the deployed WECD should be at least one month, with three months or more expected if Sea State 4 or less is maintained.

#15 [grant] Modeling UV/VIS/near-IR Observables of Dim Hypersonic Configurations
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13091
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current physical modeling tools, specifically the JANNAF EPSS suite, lack the chemical and physical mechanisms necessary to simultaneously predict at-source UV, VIS, and near-IR radiative emissions for dim hypersonic threats.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Enhancing the JANNAF suite infrastructure by adding thermal protection system response characterization, material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models, and molecular band models for UV, VIS, and near-IR radiative emission, integrated with Navier-Stokes CFD…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Hypersonic configurations (boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions at high Mach numbers across continuum and rarefied altitudes.
Abstract:
To address dim hypersonic threats in missile defense scenarios, the government desires to enhance current physical modeling tools with the ability to simultaneously predict at-source observable properties in the ultraviolet (UV), visible (VIS), and near-infrared (near-IR) spectral regimes that are founded and built upon Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) techniques and which accounts for, but is not limited to, vehicle surface heating and ablation, Arrhenius and collisional chemically reacting flows, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects, boost and divert jet exhaust interactions with the hypersonic body flowfield, and electro-optical radiative transfer physics-based models. The modeling suite provided by the Joint Army-Navy-NASA Air Force (JANNAF) Exhaust Plume and Signatures Subcommittee (EPSS) [1-4] computes RF and certain IR observables. It is founded on CFD and DSMC flowfield codes, hardbody heating models, and radiative transfer / radar propagation techniques. However, the suite does not model all the underlying chemical and physical mechanisms needed to account for radiative emissions in the identified parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Phenomenologies that must be enhanced within or added to the suite include, but are not limited to: characterization of thermal protection system response, development of material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models that consistently apply across the continuum and rarefied regimes, and generation of molecular band models for UV, Visible, and near-IR radiative emission. The developed models should be compatible with the JANNAF suite infrastructure. And the resulting assemblage should be able to model realistic hypersonic configurations (such as boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions lasting tens of minutes with high Mach within the atmosphere over a wide range of continuum and rarefied altitudes. The resulting capability is expected to facilitate the acquisition and tracking of dim hypersonic threats in modeling and simulation venues, such as MDA’s existing agency framework, and operational scenarios.

#19 [grant] Field-Friendly Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13129
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current DNN architectures suffer from 'Black Box' vulnerabilities, excessive computational scaling, lack of transparency, and a dependency on high-cost GPU infrastructure.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of an alternative to CNN-based architectures that maps parameter count to performance, replaces distributed neural layers with interpretable logic similar to standard programming code, and incorporates reliability metrics to identify when an output is unreliable.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): CNN-based image classification evaluated using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets, comparing against ResNet-18 and larger architectures on CPU and embedded edge hardware.
Abstract:
Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:

- Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.

- Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. By making input-output logic similar to standard programming code, the model should ensure decisions are easily explainable, verifiable, and compliant with auditing standards.

- Reliability: The model must recognize whether it can provide a reliable output for a given problem instance, which will address another well-known criticism of DNNs wherein performance is typically measured as an average, e.g., average accuracy, over many instances of a problem and will help build user trust and acceptability of the model vs DNNs, particularly in sensitive areas like person identification in a crowd video and identifying the source of a cyber-security violation.

The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model’s architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.

The metrics below establish outer-edge targets specifically for CNN-based image classification. While satisfying every metric is not mandatory, the model will be evaluated on the number of targets achieved and the viability of the engineering trade-offs.

1. Comparison with Base Architecture of ResNet-18 and larger

2. Comparison of the Number of Classes 10 and 100 using 3 datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, having different combinations of numbers of classes and total number of image pixels (number of channels*number of pixels per image)

3. Mean Average Accuracy of Classification: Same as DNNs or higher

4. Number of Parameters (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less

5. Training MFLOPs/Image (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less

6. Training Memory Size (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less

7. Inference MFLOPs/Image: 50% of DNNs or less

8. Rate of Growth of Metrics (5), (6), and (7): Sublinear

In Phase II, similar metrics and their extensibility and relevance to transformers and multimodality scenarios (images and videos as well as their combinations with text to form LLMs and VLMs) will need to be provided and their implementation explained.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

results.name: read_result

# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

Here's what I could put together, with the gaps flagged.

**Best-fit grant: #7 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation** (open, deadline 2027-03-31). It is the closest match to the Marine heatwave early warning project (#1): it funds strengthening and operationalising the global ocean observing system, which is exactly the observing/forecasting backbone a marine heatwave early-warning system needs. The project's own concepts (ocean data assimilation, ML for data assimilation, marine heatwave prediction, SST forecasting) line up with it. #6 (Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination, open, deadline 2027-01-31) is a secondary fit — ocean technology, but less specific to observing/forecasting. #25 (GEO Core) is open but broad and deadline-less, so it's a weaker, less targeted fit. I ruled out the rest: carbon sources/sinks (#8), Antarctica (#9), biodiversity interoperability (#10), marine geology (#11), blue forest ecosystems (#12), wave/tidal energy (#13, #14), hypersonic (#15), subsurface hazard (#16), luminescent paint (#17), marine species monitoring (#18), naval sensing (#19), field-friendly AI (#23), and the other naval/defense items — none of these match a heatwave early-warning project.

**Who should lead:** Mara Ellison (#3) — she is the PI of the lab (#20) and the project's declared interests (ocean data assimilation, marine heatwave prediction, SST forecasting) match the call's observing-system goal. Priya Raman (#26) is the strongest co-lead: her declared satellite ocean remote sensing directly supports strengthening observing capacities, and she is a lab member. Jonah Whitcombe (#27) is a weaker third (ocean particle tracking). Evidence tier: declared profile only — no demonstrated or confirmed-in-conversation evidence for any of them on this call.

**Outside the lab:** I could not finish this part. The lab-member call-fit tool only returns lab members, and I did not find a function that surfaces outside partners for a call.
