#23 [grant] Field-Friendly Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13129
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current DNN architectures suffer from 'Black Box' vulnerabilities, excessive computational scaling, lack of transparency, and a dependency on high-cost GPU infrastructure.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of an alternative to CNN-based architectures that maps parameter count to performance, replaces distributed neural layers with interpretable logic similar to standard programming code, and incorporates reliability metrics to identify when an output is unreliable.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): CNN-based image classification evaluated using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets, comparing against ResNet-18 and larger architectures on CPU and embedded edge hardware.
Abstract:
Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:

- Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.

- Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. By making input-output logic similar to standard programming code, the model should ensure decisions are easily explainable, verifiable, and compliant with auditing standards.

- Reliability: The model must recognize whether it can provide a reliable output for a given problem instance, which will address another well-known criticism of DNNs wherein performance is typically measured as an average, e.g., average accuracy, over many instances of a problem and will help build user trust and acceptability of the model vs DNNs, particularly in sensitive areas like person identification in a crowd video and identifying the source of a cyber-security violation.

The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model’s architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.

The metrics below establish outer-edge targets specifically for CNN-based image classification. While satisfying every metric is not mandatory, the model will be evaluated on the number of targets achieved and the viability of the engineering trade-offs.

1. Comparison with Base Architecture of ResNet-18 and larger

#16 [grant] Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13082
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsurface hazard detection systems suffer from a 'collect everything' bottleneck, where static, pre-programmed sensor scripts flood tactical networks with raw data, ignore environmental degradation of sensor modalities, and lack the real-time adaptability to optimize sensor tasking and rou…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

#17 [grant] Multi-Modal Luminescent Paint Systems for Underwater Surface Diagnostics
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13134
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current luminescent paint systems for underwater surface diagnostics fail to provide accurate, simultaneous, and uncoupled measurements of pressure, temperature, and skin friction due to oxygen diffusion inhibition, breakdown of Taylor's frozen-flow hypothesis, low luminous efficiency of MLPs, and …
Method (Mycelium's reading): Proposed use of innovative material architectures, such as multi-color mechano-luminescent particles or multi-core/shell dye structures, integrated with an optical processing suite to decouple cross-sensitivities.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Hydrodynamic testing in water, specifically focusing on boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces.
Abstract:
Quantifying coupled boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces require non-intrusive, full-field imaging of surface pressure, temperature, and skin friction (shear stress). While optical diagnostics have revolutionized aerodynamic testing, adapting luminescent paints to hydrodynamic testing in water introduces fundamental physical and application constraints that current state-of-the-art systems cannot overcome:

• Pressure-Sensitive Paint (PSP): Conventional PSP relies on oxygen-quenching physics. When submerged, oxygen diffusion into the polymer binder is severely inhibited by the liquid boundary layer and low oxygen solubility, rendering standard PSPs insensitive or plagued by extremely slow response times. Furthermore, severe temperature cross-sensitivity corrupts the pressure signal.

• Temperature-Sensitive Paint (TSP): Accurate dynamic temperature measurements are crippled by the standard utilization of Taylor’s frozen-flow hypothesis, which inaccurately assumes turbulent structures remain unchanged as they advect. In water, non-equilibrium flow, high thermal mass and rapid localized diffusion cause this hypothesis to break down, failing to capture true high-frequency temperature fluctuations.

• Mechano-Luminescent Paint (MLP): MLPs offer a direct optical pathway to map shear stress via mechanical deformation. However, current MLP formulations are in their technological infancy, suffering from poor dynamic range, low luminous efficiency, and signal degradation from material fatigue and hydrostatic pressure cross-talk.

In addition to the above challenges, current formulations are difficult to apply uniformly over large areas. Existing techniques fail to maintain a consistent, repeatable coating thickness on complex, curved, or non-flat surfaces. This inconsistency skews calibration and compromises measurement reliability across large-field hydrodynamic models. Innovative material architectures, such as utilizing distinct, multi-color mechano-luminescent particles or multi-core/shell dye structures, may enable simultaneous, uncoupled optical separation of pressure, shear, and temperature in all flow environments, i.e. gas, liquid, and multiphase flows.

This STTR topic seeks an integrated material, application, and optical processing suite. The system must decouple cross-sensitivities and deliver simultaneous, high dynamic range, full-field quantitative maps of the wall pressure, shear, and temperature fluctuations.

#18 [grant] Compact Unmanned Aerial System for Marine Species Monitoring
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13133
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing UAS for marine species monitoring are often prohibitively expensive, lack integrated high-resolution photogrammetry capabilities, or fail to meet specific operational requirements (size, duration, and NDAA compliance) for field-based research.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of a prototype compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS integrating a high-resolution flat zoom lens camera with a gimbal, a LiDAR altimeter/range finder (50m+), and a lightweight battery system (<100 Wh).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Small boat-based operations in wet conditions (IP45 rating) with temperatures ranging from -20 to +40 degrees Celsius.
Abstract:
A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. However, while UAS methods have led to significant advances in our understanding of marine species’ behavior, health, and body condition, thus far many obstacles remain including cost, flight duration, size, and image resolution.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS and payloads designed to collect high-resolution photogrammetry imagery to improve marine mammal monitoring, health measurements, and behavioral sequencing. In particular, the prototype device should contain the following technical parameters: high resolution flat zoom lens camera integrated with a gimbal system; highly maneuverable and flexible payload system; lightweight batteries less than 100 Watt hours; an accurate Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) altimeter and range finder integrated with the camera and capable of measuring distances up to 50m or more; and a monitor that is operational in direct sunlight and with polarized sunglasses;. It should be designed for flight times as much as or greater than 40 minutes; be compact and portable in both size and weight such that the UAS and case can fit airline luggage restrictions; have the ability to be quickly calibrated, launched, and caught by hand during small boat-based operations and to tolerate temperature range of -20 degrees to +40 degrees Celsius; and have a minimum weather resistant rating of IP45 to allow for operations in wet conditions; be capable of dynamic home point positioning; and produces minimal noise.

While there are several existing NDAA-compliant drones available in the marketplace, the desired components and capabilities only exist in piecemeal and further, these UAS are prohibitively expensive for the field. The DON seeks to develop a prototype device to be designed and optimized for marine species monitoring, encompassing all the above technical parameters. Critically, this device must be affordable for the marine research community with the target market price between $10,000 - $15,000.

#19 [grant] Distributed Multispectral Event-Driven Integrated Sensing and Communications
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13104
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current frame-based processing for remote passive sensors generates large data volumes, causing high energy consumption, processing bottlenecks, and communication delays that hinder time-critical battlespace awareness in resource-limited hardware platforms.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Multispectral Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications (MINSC), an event-driven, asynchronous sensing and processing framework utilizing neuromorphic computing for energy-efficient edge inference and low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) data transmission.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Navy Aegis Combat System (ACS) and Aegis Test Bed (ATB) environments for cross-domain operations and remote passive sensing.
Abstract:
The Navy Aegis Program Office is interested in expanding battlespace awareness to support cross-domain operations through the integration of remote passive sensors. Currently, these sensors rely on real-time frame-based processing that generates large volumes of data, requiring significant processing power and energy and creating constraints for resource-limited hardware platforms with finite battery life, processing capabilities, and memory. In addition, transmitting large volumes of data over dynamic communication links can introduce delays and encounter bandwidth limitations that cannot meet time-critical operational needs. The complexity of the battlespace and electromagnetic environment further presents challenges for robust detection, classification, and identification. Advanced remote passive-sensor technologies that enable efficient and distributed sensing and processing will support multidomain operations by providing timely and resilient battlespace awareness. Successful technologies will be transitioned to the Aegis Combat System (ACS) to enhance distributed sensing, accelerate decision-making, and enable cross-domain operations.

The Navy is seeking to develop Multispectral Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications (MINSC) technology to support endurant remote sensing capability. MINSC is an event-driven sensor featuring low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) data transmission that can timely identify a wide range of objects and transmit the information to remote platforms to integrate into the existing decision-making process. Neuromorphic computing can provide energy efficient, parallel processing, and low-latency framework for passive sensing, edge computing, and remote inference.

Neuromorphic sensors deliver high temporal resolution, asynchronous, energy and bandwidth efficient data inspired by biological vision. The Navy seeks to build an Event-Driven Energy-Efficient Ecosystem to support Endurant Long-Range Sensing and Communications capability. Solutions can be software, neuromorphic hardware, and/or end-to-end neuromorphic system that can deliver robust information and fuse with existing sensors to provide improved tracking, detection, classification, and identification. The Navy is open to innovative ideas of novel system design that can make decisions locally and communicate sparingly or timely send out the event-driven information for remote inference. The intended capability is an integrated remote passive-sensing capability that performs event-driven local sensing and processing, communicating only the information necessary to enhance remote awareness, and fuses with existing sensors to improve tracking, detection, classification and identification.

Distributed MINSC will provide advantages in dynamic environment and resilience to noise and debris associated with military applications. Incorporating event-based multispectral remote sensors with onboard sensors will expand operational battlespace, contribute to robust Common Operational Picture (COP) and enhance situational awareness. It will integrate with the Aegis and permit realistic testing of all threat types and configurations in a dynamic testing environment. Track visualization will be delivered through the existing ACS console Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs). The solution will support current operator track management and decision-making and integrate with the AEGIS Test Bed (ATB) to facilitate system evaluation against more advanced threats. The solution will provide an enhanced capability to address targets in all configurations and optimal engagement options to the sailors, which will increase mission capability and effectiveness against the latest threats.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable

You're right to flag it — I cited #2 (Marine heatwave early warning) but the read of it was cleared from my view, so I cannot honestly re-state its problem, method, or milestones from what I can see now. What I can say is what I did read: the project's concepts (marine heatwave prediction, ocean data assimilation, subseasonal forecasting, ocean data dashboards) and that 2 of its concepts are held by no member's declared profile — sea surface temperature and fisheries work. I cannot honestly claim to have read its full description, milestones, or budget.

So the fit conclusion stands only in outline, not as a verified read: #23 (Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate) is the strongest fit on the evidence I have — it is about predicting extreme events, welcomes AI-based approaches and high-resolution models, and its deadline (2027-03-04) is after the project's current slate items. But I have not verified #2's milestones against that deadline, and I have not confirmed #23 is open or eligible for the lab.

- Reading #2 in full (its description, milestones, budget) — the read was cleared and I cannot see it now.
- Confirming #23's eligibility, amount, or whether the lab is eligible — I saw the abstract/scope and deadline, not the eligibility rules.
- Naming an outside-lab partner — collaborator search is off, and I have no consented outside people to suggest.
- Confirming anyone's consent to be named as lead.

Here's where things stand, with the limits flagged.

**Best fit: #23 — Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate** (€3,000,000–€15,000,000, deadline 2027-03-04, still open). It is the only call in the project's slate-adjacent set that is about predicting extreme events, and it explicitly welcomes AI-based approaches, high-resolution models, and subseasonal-to-multi-decadal prediction — the exact shape of #2 Marine heatwave early warning (marine heatwave prediction, ocean data assimilation, subseasonal forecasting). One plain reason: it is built for what the project does. One plain doubt: the project's slate (#2's current slate, all 10 items) does not include #23, so it is not a slate-ranked item — it came up via search, not via the project's own slate.

The runner-up is #7 — A stronger Global Ocean Observing System (€50,000,000, deadline 2027-02-16). It is about strengthening observing systems, not heatwave prediction; Mara and Priya both cover its one slot, but it is a broader, observing-system-scale call, not an early-warning call. #6 (Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination) is instrumentation development — nobody in the lab covers it, so it is a weak fit.

**Who should lead: Tomás Ferreira-Lind (#4).** He is the only lab member whose declared profile covers a slot in #23 — "high resolution Earth system models" (declared: regional ocean models). Mara (#3) is the PI and declared ocean extremes and data assimilation, but the call's slot is Tomás's, and the nightly ranking puts Tomás ahead of Mara and Jonah. I would not name Mara as the lead on the call itself; she is the PI and should co-lead, but the application lead should be Tomás. Gaps no one covers: prediction of extreme events in a changing climate, digital twins, Copernicus, Galileo/EGNOS.

**Outside-lab partner: I cannot name one.** Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, and I have no consented outside-lab people to suggest. The call itself encourages cooperation with Copernicus/Destination Earth-type actors and low- to middle-income countries, but those are roles, not people — I won't invent names. If you want, you can ask the lab to enable collaborator search or ask Tomás/Mara directly who they'd want on the consortium.

**What I could not finish:** I did not read the full text of #23 beyond the abstract/scope, did not check eligibility (citizenship, institution type, career stage) — none of that is visible to me — and I did not verify #23's position in the lab's full 31-item slate (I only saw the first 16). I also did not confirm anyone's consent to be named.

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

Scope:

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Utilizing a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), data from past and recent climate, AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, and case studies to improve prediction, projection, and attribution capabilities across s…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe and globally, encompassing large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena, with specific focus on EU and national/regional actors, low- to middle-income countries, and integration with initiatives like Copernicus and Destination Earth.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

results.name: read_result
results.content:
# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

final_text:
I have what I need. Here's the picture.

**Best fit: #8 — Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity** (€3,000,000–€8,000,000, deadline 2027-09-22, still open). It is the only call in #2's slate that matches the project's method: satellite detections integrated with in-situ observations, delivered as an interoperable data framework. The project's own focus — floating debris detection and beaching — is not what the call is about, though: it is biodiversity-focused, and its scope is ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities, not marine litter. So it is the closest fit, not a clean one. The other slate items are off-topic for #2 (carbon, Antarctica, blue forests, wave/tidal energy, subsea power, maternal health, geology, instrumentation, global observing system).

**Who should lead: Priya Raman (#4).** She is the only lab member who covers a requirement slot for #8 — "satellite-based Earth observation data" (declared: satellite ocean remote sensing). The nightly ranking also names her, noting her satellite ocean colour and harmful algal bloom work as a direct application of integrating remote sensing for biodiversity. Sun-hee Park (#17) is named by the ranking for the interoperable data framework side (web GIS and data dashboards), but she is not a member of #2 and her coverage is not declared for this call. Jonah Whitcombe (#5) is the project's litter/Lagrangian specialist but covers no slot for #8. Mara (#3) is the PI and project lead but covers no slot for #8 either.

**Gaps:** the call asks for in-situ data collection frameworks (e.g., GBIF, OBIS, LUCAS) and machine learning / omics-based data — no one in the lab covers these. The project's own concepts (floating debris detection, Lagrangian particle tracking) are held by no member's declared profile — a gap to fill or a profile to update.

**Outside the lab:** I cannot name anyone outside the lab. Collaborator search is turned off on this instance, and no outside person has consented to be suggested. The only outside-the-lab names the ranking surfaced are Sun-hee Park (#17) — who is actually in the lab — and no external collaborators. If you want outside partners, you'd need to enable collaborator search or ask the lab to identify candidates.

**One doubt:** #8 is biodiversity-framed, so the debris-tracking core of #2 may not fit its scope cleanly; the fit is strongest on the satellite-plus-in-situ integration, weakest on the litter-specific science. Worth checking the call's eligibility and scope against the project's actual deliverables before committing.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

#8 [grant] Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

#11 [grant] Large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems in European sea basins
Amount: €1,000,000–€8,925,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-MISS-2027-03-OCEAN-05
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-21
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration, and management of blue forest ecosystems (marine and coastal vegetated habitats) within European sea basins to meet EU climate, biodiversity, and restoration goals.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Innovative multidisciplinary projects integrating active and passive restoration, conservation efforts (e.g., managing Marine Protected Areas), innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., nature credits), multi-sensor research and monitoring, and community engagement, tailored to specific sea basins.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European sea basins, specifically one of four 'lighthouse' areas: Atlantic and Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic and North Sea, or Danube River basin (including Black Sea), involving EU Member States and Associated Countries.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Increased area and improved condition of marine and coastal vegetated habitats within EU waters through effective on-site conservation, restoration and management of activities to help deliver on the objectives of the Nature Restoration Regulation;

- Maintained and enhanced capacity of blue carbon ecosystems to naturally store carbon, supporting EU climate mitigation goals;

- Enhanced capacity of marine vegetated habitats/blue carbon ecosystems to support biodiversity and fisheries;

- Established novel financing and incentive mechanisms that support conservation, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems projects;

- Raised public awareness and improved community participation in blue forest ecosystems protection, restoration and management activities, ensuring long-term involvement.

Scope:

This topic seeks innovative multidisciplinary projects that will advance large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems, focusing on the assessment of ecological interactions, restoration of degraded ecosystems, conservation, and sustainable management within European sea basins. Projects are required to develop collaborations with EU Member States and Associated Countries national and regional agencies and authorities and policy makers and engage with local communities, researchers and NGOs. #14 [grant] Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13137
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsea ISR nodes and UUV docking stations rely on lithium-chemistry batteries that suffer from capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess toxic chemistries, and require resource-intensive physical replacement in contested or ice-covered environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters that generate electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between anoxic marine sediment and oxygenated overlying seawater, utilizing abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Sub-zero Arctic subsea environments, specifically the interface between marine sediment and overlying seawater.
Abstract:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:

While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

#14 [grant] Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13137
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsea ISR nodes and UUV docking stations rely on lithium-chemistry batteries that suffer from capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess toxic chemistries, and require resource-intensive physical replacement in contested or ice-covered environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters that generate electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between anoxic marine sediment and oxygenated overlying seawater, utilizing abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Sub-zero Arctic subsea environments, specifically the interface between marine sediment and overlying seawater.
Abstract:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:

While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

I have what I need. Here's where things stand.

## Where Plastic pathways stands (#2)

- **Focus:** tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups.
- **Status:** satellite debris detections run weekly; the beaching model is being checked against last summer's beach surveys.
- **Progress:** 35%.
- **State:** never confirmed by its members — so this is the last recorded state, not a fresh check. Worth confirming with Priya and Jonah before relying on it.
- **Members:** Mara (#3), Priya (#4), Jonah (#5). No open blockers are recorded in the project state.

## Three most relevant new papers

1. **#15** — *Code and aggregated results for "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter…"* (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). Directly on your beaching model: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels 3.1.4, applied to field records from Uido, Korea, with ROMS flow fields. This is the closest match to your current check against beach surveys.
2. **#12** — *Supporting Data for Satellite Observations of River Plumes and Wind Response in Neighboring Bays on Iceland's Northeast Coast* (Whitney & Glass, 2026, Mendeley Data). Satellite (Sentinel-2 True Color, Sentinel-3 TSM) observations of river plumes and wind response — directly relevant to your river-mouth-to-beach detection work.
3. **#10** — *Chlorophyll-a estimation from Sentinel-2 data using in-context learning with a tabular foundation model* (Basit, Moser & Serpico, 2026). Not debris detection itself, but it shows how Sentinel-2 time series can be turned into usable estimates with in-context learning — a method you could adapt for debris detection rather than chlorophyll.

(#11, hyperspectral HAB detection, is also remote-sensing-adjacent but targets algae, not debris — I'd rank it below these three.)

## One funding opportunity

**#29 — Oil Spill Recovery Institute (OSRI) Graduate Research Fellowship** (deadline 2027-01-08, open). It supports graduate research on spill detection and tracking, with emphasis on spill detection and tracking, and offers up to two years for master's or four for doctoral students.

- **What fits:** your project is exactly about tracking floating debris from river mouths to beaches — the same detection-and-tracking problem, and the fellowship explicitly names spill detection and tracking as an area of emphasis.
- **Biggest doubt:** it is a *graduate* fellowship, not a lab grant — it would fund one person's research, not the lab's weekly detection pipeline. If you want lab-level funding, the closer fit would be a grant like **#17 (Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination)** or **#18 (Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity)**, but those are broader and #18 is biodiversity-focused, so neither is a clean match either.
- **What I could not check:** eligibility (citizenship, institution type, career stage) — the call does not state it in what I read.

If you want, I can also look at the fellowship slate further down (offset=10) or check who in the lab is at graduate stage and could apply.

#10 [paper] Chlorophyll-a estimation from Sentinel-2 data using in-context learning with a tabular foundation model
Authors: Abdul Basit, Gabriele Moser, Sebastiano B. Serpico
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3116961
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The non-linear relationship between surface reflectance and in-situ Chlorophyll-a (CHL-a) measurements, which varies based on seasonal conditions, temporal dynamics, and environmental changes.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A hybrid context construction approach combining seasonal consistency and spectral similarity to select historical samples for a transformer-based tabular foundation model (TabICLv2) performing in-context learning.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Time series Sentinel-2 observations and corresponding in-situ CHL-a measurements from the Ligurian sea, Italy.
Abstract:
Chlorophyll-a (CHL-a) concentration is a crucial environmental parameter for monitoring marine and freshwater ecosystems. As a biological indicator, it measures the levels of CHL-a, a green pigment that reflects the presence of phytoplankton in aquatic environments. Remote sensing is a powerful tool for monitoring the spatial distribution of CHL-a concentration. In particular, multispectral data acquired by passive optical sensors can be used to model the relationship between surface reflectance and in-situ CHL-a measurements collected during field visits. However, this relationship is highly non-linear and varies with seasonal conditions, temporal dynamics, and environmental changes. This paper proposes a formulation of a tabular foundation model based on a hybrid context construction approach for online CHL-a estimation, combining seasonal consistency and spectral similarity to select informative historical samples. The approach is implemented using a transformer-based tabular foundation model, TabICLv2, which performs prediction through in-context learning. For each query sample, a fixed number of relevant observations are dynamically retrieved and used as contextual input for inference. A dataset comprising time series Sentinel-2 observations and corresponding in-situ CHL-a measurements of the Ligurian sea, Italy, was constructed. Experiments were performed by comparing both with alternative formulations of TabICLv2 and with traditional machine learning models, including Random Forest (RF) and Adaptive Random Forest (ARF, with a Hoeffding tree as the base learner). While all models benefit from selecting a fixed number of relevant samples, the improvement is more pronounced for TabICLv2, which achieves the best overall performance. These findings highlight the importance of structured context selection and demonstrate the potential of in-context learning for temporally dynamic remote sensing applications.

#11 [paper] Hyperspectral remote sensing for harmful algal bloom detection: Pseudo-nitzschia in the Northeast Pacific.
Authors: Bailess, Alexander L, Baetge, Nicholas, Barnard, Andrew H, Tufillaro, Nicholas, Behrenfeld, Michael, Bill, Brian, Kudela, Raphael, Graff, Jason
Venue: Harmful algae
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43020539/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for rapid, scalable identification of harmful algal blooms, specifically Pseudo-nitzschia, to manage marine resources, given that current in-situ point sampling methods are expensive and labor-intensive.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Culturing four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, measuring their hyperspectral absorption and backscatter, modeling spectral reflectances detectable by remote sensing platforms, and quantifying differences between taxonomic fingerprints using vector-based and stat…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including Pseudo-nitzschia, Thalassiosira, Chaetoceros, and Asterionellopsis.
Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

final_text:
Here's where Plastic pathways stands, based on what I can see.

**Where it stands**
- #2 Plastic pathways (scope: lab): tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups.
- Status: satellite debris detections run weekly; the beaching model is being checked against last summer's beach surveys. Progress: 35%.
- State: never confirmed by its members — so the 35% and the "weekly detections" line are unverified; worth confirming with Priya Raman (#4) and Jonah Whitcombe (#5).
- Blockers: none recorded in the project record. The one open-ended item is the beaching-model validation against last summer's surveys.

**Three most relevant new papers** (all in the slate, all new this week)
- #12 — Supporting Data for Satellite Observations of River Plumes and Wind Response in Neighboring Bays on Iceland's Northeast Coast: Sentinel-2 True Color and Sentinel-3 TSM imagery of river plumes and wind response — the closest match to the project's river-mouth-to-beach framing.
- #10 — Chlorophyll-a estimation from Sentinel-2 data using in-context learning with a tabular foundation model: Sentinel-2 time-series estimation with in-context learning — directly relevant to the satellite-detection side.
- #11 — Hyperspectral remote sensing for harmful algal bloom detection: Pseudo-nitzschia in the Northeast Pacific: hyperspectral fingerprinting for scalable detection — relevant to the detection method, though it's about blooms rather than debris.

**One funding opportunity**
- #18 — Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity, towards a fully interoperable observation and data framework (€3,000,000–€8,000,000, deadline 2027-09-22): it asks for exactly the integration the project does — satellite remote sensing plus in-situ observations (here, beach surveys) — and it explicitly covers marine ecosystems and data integration for predictive analytics. It's a fit for the lab's satellite-detection + beach-survey pipeline, though it's biodiversity-framed, so the pitch would need to lean on the debris/beaching angle.
- A second option worth noting: #17 — Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (deadline 2027-02-15), for instrumentation development — relevant if the lab wants to build or improve detection hardware.

One caveat: the slate is partial (papers 1–10 of 110, fellowships 1–10 of 25), so I've only seen the top of the ranked list. Also, #29 (OSRI Graduate Research Fellowship, deadline 2027-01-08) is flagged in the slate as "Perfect Alignment for Spill Tracking" — but it's a fellowship for a graduate student, not a project grant, so it's a person-level opportunity, not a project funding route.

Next steps I'd suggest: confirm the project state with the team, and if you want, I can pull the rest of the slate or dig into #18's full scope.

#10 [paper] Chlorophyll-a estimation from Sentinel-2 data using in-context learning with a tabular foundation model
Authors: Abdul Basit, Gabriele Moser, Sebastiano B. Serpico
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3116961
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The non-linear relationship between surface reflectance and in-situ Chlorophyll-a (CHL-a) measurements, which varies based on seasonal conditions, temporal dynamics, and environmental changes.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A hybrid context construction approach combining seasonal consistency and spectral similarity to select historical samples for a transformer-based tabular foundation model (TabICLv2) performing in-context learning.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Time series Sentinel-2 observations and corresponding in-situ CHL-a measurements from the Ligurian sea, Italy.
Abstract:
Chlorophyll-a (CHL-a) concentration is a crucial environmental parameter for monitoring marine and freshwater ecosystems. As a biological indicator, it measures the levels of CHL-a, a green pigment that reflects the presence of phytoplankton in aquatic environments. Remote sensing is a powerful tool for monitoring the spatial distribution of CHL-a concentration. In particular, multispectral data acquired by passive optical sensors can be used to model the relationship between surface reflectance and in-situ CHL-a measurements collected during field visits. However, this relationship is highly non-linear and varies with seasonal conditions, temporal dynamics, and environmental changes. This paper proposes a formulation of a tabular foundation model based on a hybrid context construction approach for online CHL-a estimation, combining seasonal consistency and spectral similarity to select informative historical samples. The approach is implemented using a transformer-based tabular foundation model, TabICLv2, which performs prediction through in-context learning. For each query sample, a fixed number of relevant observations are dynamically retrieved and used as contextual input for inference. A dataset comprising time series Sentinel-2 observations and corresponding in-situ CHL-a measurements of the Ligurian sea, Italy, was constructed. Experiments were performed by comparing both with alternative formulations of TabICLv2 and with traditional machine learning models, including Random Forest (RF) and Adaptive Random Forest (ARF, with a Hoeffding tree as the base learner). While all models benefit from selecting a fixed number of relevant samples, the improvement is more pronounced for TabICLv2, which achieves the best overall performance. These findings highlight the importance of structured context selection and demonstrate the potential of in-context learning for temporally dynamic remote sensing applications.

#11 [paper] Hyperspectral remote sensing for harmful algal bloom detection: Pseudo-nitzschia in the Northeast Pacific.
Authors: Bailess, Alexander L, Baetge, Nicholas, Barnard, Andrew H, Tufillaro, Nicholas, Behrenfeld, Michael, Bill, Brian, Kudela, Raphael, Graff, Jason
Venue: Harmful algae
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43020539/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for rapid, scalable identification of harmful algal blooms, specifically Pseudo-nitzschia, to manage marine resources, given that current in-situ point sampling methods are expensive and labor-intensive.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Culturing four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, measuring their hyperspectral absorption and backscatter, modeling spectral reflectances detectable by remote sensing platforms, and quantifying differences between taxonomic fingerprints using vector-based and stat…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including Pseudo-nitzschia, Thalassiosira, Chaetoceros, and Asterionellopsis.
Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.

Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

final_text:
Here's where #2 Plastic pathways stands, what's new in its slate, and one funding angle.

**Where it stands**
- Focus: tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches with forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups.
- Status: satellite debris detections run weekly; the beaching model is being checked against last summer's beach surveys.
- Progress: 35%.
- State: never confirmed by its members — so treat the 35% and the status line as unverified, not as a confirmed picture. No blockers are recorded in the project record.
- Members: #3 Mara Ellison (PI), #4 Priya Raman, #5 Jonah Whitcombe.

**Three most relevant new papers** (all in the slate this week or earlier):
- #15 — Code and aggregated results for "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter" (Uido, Republic of Korea). Directly on the beaching model: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels 3.1.4, with scripts and aggregated results. This is the closest match to the project's core method.
- #12 — Supporting data for satellite observations of river plumes and wind response in neighboring bays (Iceland). Satellite-based tracking of river-mouth plumes — the "river mouths" end of the project's scope.
- #10 — Chlorophyll-a estimation from Sentinel-2 using in-context learning with a tabular foundation model. A Sentinel-2-based estimation method — the closest slate item to the project's satellite-detection side, though it targets chlorophyll-a, not debris.

I'd note #11 (hyperspectral HAB detection) is also satellite-detection-adjacent but is about algal blooms, not debris, so it ranks below #10 for this project.

**One funding opportunity**
#18 — Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity (Horizon Europe, €3M–€8M, deadline 2027-09-22, still open). It asks for multisensory integration of in-situ and satellite data with FAIR data and AI analytics — a reasonable fit for the project's satellite-detection + in-situ beach-survey combination. The biggest doubt: it is framed around biodiversity/ecosystem condition, not marine litter, so the fit is indirect — you'd need to argue debris tracking as an ecosystem-monitoring use case. The strongest reason to look at it is the satellite-plus-in-situ integration angle; the biggest doubt is that the call's scope is biodiversity, not litter.

One thing I could not check: eligibility (institution type, consortium rules, budget) — that's in the call's full text, not in the slate summary. Also worth noting: the project's state has never been confirmed, so before applying, the team should confirm the current state and blockers in the app.
